A Conductor Moving Through a Magnetic Field

There is a beautifully intuitive way to understand Faraday’s Law that does not require any calculus of flux: consider the force on charges in a conductor that moves through a magnetic field.

A straight conductor of length \(L\) moves with velocity \(\vec{v}\) perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) (say, \(\vec{B}\) points into the page). The free electrons inside the conductor experience a magnetic force:

\[\vec{F} = q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}\]

This force pushes electrons toward one end of the conductor, leaving the other end positive. Charge accumulates until the electric field from the separated charges exactly balances the magnetic force:

\[qE = qvB \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad E = vB\]

The potential difference between the ends is:

\[\boxed{\mathcal{E} = BLv}\]

This is the motional EMF — a voltage that appears across a conductor simply because it moves through a magnetic field. No battery, no changing external field — just motion.

The Sliding Rail Problem

The most important application: a conducting rod slides at constant velocity \(v\) along parallel rails separated by distance \(L\), connected by a resistor \(R\) at one end, all in a uniform field \(\vec{B}\) (into the page).

As the rod moves, the area of the closed circuit increases: \(A = Lx\), where \(x\) is the rod’s position. The flux is \(\Phi_B = BLx\), and:

\[\mathcal{E} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt} = -BL\frac{dx}{dt} = -BLv\]

The magnitude of the induced EMF is \(|\mathcal{E}| = BLv\), confirming our force-based derivation. The induced current is:

\[I = \frac{|\mathcal{E}|}{R} = \frac{BLv}{R}\]

By Lenz’s Law, the current flows counterclockwise (to oppose the increasing flux into the page). This current-carrying rod in the magnetic field experiences a braking force:

\[F = BIL = \frac{B^2L^2v}{R}\]

This force opposes the motion. To maintain constant velocity, an external agent must apply an equal force, doing work at rate:

\[P_\text{external} = Fv = \frac{B^2L^2v^2}{R}\]

The power dissipated in the resistor is:

\[P_R = I^2R = \frac{B^2L^2v^2}{R}\]

They are equal: all the mechanical work done by the external agent is converted to electrical energy dissipated as heat in the resistor. Energy conservation is satisfied exactly.

*Personal note: This is the physics of regenerative braking. When an electric car decelerates, the wheels drive a generator backward through the magnetic field. The braking force (which slows the car) does work that charges the battery instead of heating brake pads. The sliding rail is the same thing, stripped to its essence.

Example: Motional EMF on Sliding Rails

A rod slides at \(v = 5.0\ \text{m/s}\) on rails separated by \(L = 0.40\ \text{m}\) in a field \(B = 0.80\ \text{T}\). The resistance is \(R = 2.0\ \Omega\).

(A) Induced EMF:

\[|\mathcal{E}| = BLv = (0.80)(0.40)(5.0) = \boxed{1.6\ \text{V}}\]

(B) Induced current:

\[I = |\mathcal{E}|/R = 1.6/2.0 = \boxed{0.80\ \text{A}}\]

(C) Force required to maintain constant velocity:

\[F = BIL = (0.80)(0.80)(0.40) = \boxed{0.256\ \text{N}}\]

(D) Power balance:

\[P_\text{mech} = Fv = (0.256)(5.0) = 1.28\ \text{W}\]

\[P_R = I^2R = (0.80)^2(2.0) = 1.28\ \text{W} \quad \checkmark\]

Eddy Currents

When a bulk conductor (not just a thin wire) moves through a nonuniform magnetic field, the changing flux induces circulating currents throughout the conductor called eddy currents. These currents:

  • Flow in closed loops within the conductor
  • Obey Lenz’s Law: they create fields opposing the flux change
  • Produce a braking force that opposes the relative motion
  • Dissipate energy as \(I^2R\) heating in the conductor

Applications:

  • Magnetic braking: Drop a strong magnet through a copper tube — the magnet falls slowly because eddy currents create an upward force. No friction, no contact, no wear.
  • Induction cooktops: A rapidly alternating magnetic field induces eddy currents in the steel pot. The pot heats from \(I^2R\) losses while the cooktop surface stays cool.
  • Metal detectors: A coil produces an alternating field; eddy currents in a metal object alter the field pattern, which the detector senses.

Example: The Falling Magnet

A small neodymium magnet (mass \(m = 5.0\ \text{g}\)) is dropped through a vertical copper pipe. It reaches a terminal velocity of \(v_t = 0.10\ \text{m/s}\) (compared to free-fall speed after the same distance, which would be several m/s).

At terminal velocity, the magnetic braking force equals gravity:

\[F_\text{brake} = mg = (0.005)(9.8) = 0.049\ \text{N}\]

The power dissipated as heat in the copper pipe walls is:

\[P = F_\text{brake}\cdot v_t = (0.049)(0.10) = \boxed{4.9\ \text{mW}}\]

The gravitational potential energy of the magnet is being converted entirely into ohmic heating of the copper pipe — through electromagnetic induction with no physical contact between magnet and pipe.
